author: Chintan Vaghela
tagline: Every service's local and public URL on one card, beside the live health of the box running them.
description:
Service Dash turns an existing Uptime Kuma status page into a homelab
dashboard. Each service gets one card carrying both of its addresses --
the internal (local) URL you use at home and the external (public) URL you
use away from it -- so you open either one without keeping a second
bookmark list. Each card opens whichever address the browser you are
holding can actually reach -- LAN at home, public when you are out --
decided per card, with a manual switch still there if you want it.

The pairing comes from Uptime Kuma itself: two monitors named `Plex` and
`Plex local` become one card with two addresses. Nothing to configure --
name the monitors that way and the card builds itself.

Alongside the cards, an embedded Netdata Agent reports the health of the
host itself: CPU, RAM, storage and live network throughput, plus the
LAN and WAN addresses of the machine, detected automatically.

**What it does**

- Local and public URLs on one card, opening whichever one you can reach
- Live up/down state pulled straight from your Uptime Kuma status page
- Host CPU, RAM, storage and network throughput from a bundled Netdata Agent
- Around 2,900 service icons, searchable, or paste an image link
- Per-card icon and Docker container mapping, shared across every browser
- A shared notes panel, gated behind your Uptime Kuma sign-in
- Addresses stay locked signed out, and unreadable until pointed at signed in
- Optional: how much of your Claude or ChatGPT plan is left, on the wall
- No build step, no account, no telemetry -- static files behind nginx

**Requires an Uptime Kuma instance already running on this host.** See the
installation tips before installing.

**Learn more:** [Service Dash on GitHub](https://github.com/cvaghela/service-dash)

tips.before_install:
### Before you install

Service Dash reads your monitors from **Uptime Kuma**. It does not
install Kuma for you, so set that up first:

1. Install **Uptime Kuma** -- it is in the official ZimaOS app store --
   and leave it on its default port `3001`. If you run it on another
   port, change `KUMA_PORT` below and `KUMA_URL` on the `kuma-auth`
   service to match. Kuma must be on this same host.
2. In Uptime Kuma, create a **status page** and add the monitors you
   want on the dashboard.
3. Note the status page's **slug** -- the last part of its URL. If it is
   not `homelab`, change `STATUS_SLUG` below to match.

### Getting local and public URLs on one card

Both addresses come from Uptime Kuma, from **how you name the
monitors**. Give a service two monitors:

| Monitor name | Points at | Shows on the card as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Plex` | your public URL | **External** |
| `Plex local` | your LAN URL | **Local** |

Service Dash pairs them by name into a single card carrying both.
`Plex (local)`, `Plex - local` and `Plex.local` are recognised the same
way. A service with only one monitor simply shows one address.

Each address is the monitor's own URL in Kuma, so it is set in Kuma, not
here. The dashboard opens whichever address your browser can actually
reach -- the local one when you are on the LAN, the public one when you
are not -- deciding per card and without testing anything. The switch in
the top bar pins it to **Local** or **External** if you would rather
choose yourself.

Both addresses read **URL Locked** until you sign in to Uptime Kuma from
the dashboard -- signed out, they are never sent to the browser at all.

Then open Service Dash on port **8888**.

title: Service Dash
release_note:
1.5.1 makes the AI usage panel actually reachable on ZimaOS. 1.5.0
shipped its two reporters behind a Compose profile, and CasaOS silently
drops any service that declares one -- so the panel could not be turned
on at all, by update or by fresh install. They are now ordinary services
that sit idle until you sign in, so enabling the feature is just:

  sudo docker exec -it service-dash-claude-usage claude auth login

Idle they cost about 12MB of RAM and no measurable CPU. The trade is
disk: both images carry a vendor CLI and are pulled whether or not you
use them.

Also in this cycle, from 1.5.0: the AI usage panel itself -- how much of
your Claude and ChatGPT plan is left, as dials above the grid -- plus a
fix for iPhone Safari killing the tab after a few minutes of scrolling,
and dialogs no longer running under the notch.
